What does his guidance depend on?), Activities 2–3 in pairs; 31–38 Use: Learners write an evidence-to-stance paragraph about a popular belief tested by evidence (for example that sugar gives lasting energy), with one if … will sentence, one passive and “while in fact”; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What pattern repeats in the moon and sun verses, and how does the last verse end it?
What is the difference between how people treated the heavenly bodies and what the writer says they are?
What did Abraham demonstrate in the debate?
interactiveTips: Use “The Moon and the Sun” hotspot for the moon and the sun and the “A Debate About the Stars” hotspot for the debate with the star worshippers.
Replay the verse from the sun to the end and ask learners to note the words of the declaration.
Do not ask learners to extend the theology beyond the chapter’s sentences.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frames “When he saw ____ rising, he said ____. When it set, he said ____.” and “They were worshipped by people, while in fact ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a paragraph that contrasts appearance and reality twice, once with “while in fact” and once with “however”, and explain the difference in position.

formativeAssessment: Follows the verse pattern accurately.
Explains the conditional as a dependency, not a confession.
Chooses active or passive for focus and uses “while in fact” to correct.
expectedResponses: When the moon and the sun set, Abraham rejected them and declared he was not of the idolaters; the writer says the heavenly bodies were worshipped by people, while in fact they had been created and appear and disappear at the Creator’s command.
content.transferTask: Write two sentences about a common belief: One passive sentence about how it is treated and one “while in fact” sentence that corrects it with evidence.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover the job of the passive and of “while in fact” from the practice-versus-reality question, and did they read the verses respectfully?

classroomManagement.instructions: Fill the rising and setting boxes from the verses. Then think, pair and share: what did people do, and what does the writer say was really true?
checkQuestions: What two boxes do you fill? (rising and setting)
What do you find in pairs? (the two passives and the linking phrase)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that pairs find “while in fact” as the link. In Activity 1, listen for the idea that Abraham’s guidance depends on his Lord. In the Use task, check one if … will, one passive and one “while in fact”.

exitTicket: Write one “If …, I will …” sentence and one “… while in fact …” sentence about a school topic.

rubricLevels.secure: Follows the verse pattern accurately.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the three heavenly bodies in order.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains the conditional as dependence, not confession.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Is he lost, or saying what guidance depends on?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Chooses active or passive for focus.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What do we want first in the sentence?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses “while in fact” to correct a belief.

interculturalFocus.notice: The chapter corrects a belief: Heavenly bodies were worshipped, while in fact they had been created. Many ancient cultures worshipped the sun or moon.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which ancient cultures had sun or moon gods (Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Incas)? Which English weekday names still carry old sky gods (Sunday, Monday)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners use neutral historical language ('they believed', 'they worshipped') and avoid insulting words about past peoples.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note the moon, the sun and the debate.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners explain in three sentences what Abraham showed in the debate.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner explains to a partner why heavenly bodies cannot be partners with Allah. The partner gives one reason.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Questioner asks “What appeared and disappeared at the Creator’s command?”. Finder reads the answer. Summarizer paraphrases it.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A classmate asks, “Do people in your country watch the moon for special days?” The learner answers and links it to the chapter.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “His young heart was filled with severe pain.” into their home language. How did each pair render “severe”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what Abraham understood about the sun and the moon. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The writer adds ‘(i.e., Allah)’ in brackets. Why?” (It makes the meaning clear.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners explain the debate in their own words and do not translate the verses.

objectives: Explain the chapter’s contrast between created heavenly bodies and Allah, who is everlasting.
State Abraham’s two-part clarification: The heavenly bodies are unworthy of worship and they are signs of Allah.

Discover how passive participles describe created things, how “However” marks the contrast between the created and the Creator, and how firstly … secondly and not only … but also organize a two-part argument.
Connect rational thinking with the start of the conflict without adding events.
content.pedagogy: Start from the words that describe the heavenly bodies: learners collect “created, controlled, managed, made to serve a purpose, come and go” and notice that almost every one describes something done to them. You then ask: “Who or what is on the other side of ‘However’?” and learners discover that the contrast is between created things and the Creator. The two-part clarification becomes a two-box organiser (not gods / signs), which leads naturally to “not only that … but also that …”. The verse is read and explained, not gapped.
priorKnowledge: Past participles as adjectives; however; firstly / secondly.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “However” does not contrast Abraham with the worshippers here; it contrasts the heavenly bodies with Allah.
The chapter does not only reject the heavenly bodies as gods; it also presents them as signs of Allah.
The conflict starts after the clarification; the chapter ends as the people begin arguing and threatening.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: passive participles for created things (created, controlled, managed, and made to serve a purpose) · un- = not (unworthy) · However for the created / Creator contrast · firstly … secondly … → not only that … but also that … · and then … → After / Once + clause.
Notice (Activities 1–2): after matching the descriptions, ask: “Do the heavenly bodies act in these words, or is something done to them?” Then read the two sentences around “However” and ask: “What is on each side of the contrast?”
Build (Activity 3): Rewrite the two-part clarification with not only that … but also that … and turn “…, and then …” into a time clause with After / Once / When.
Likely errors: *not only the heavenly bodies are unworthy … but also (missing that / word order) · *After Abraham’s thinking helped …, then the conflict started · However read as Abraham vs the people.
Use (Activity 4): an 8–10 sentence paragraph on a non-story topic where something visible is evaluated and then reinterpreted, with one passive description, one however, firstly / secondly and a final consequence.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Four participles as a list, the last one longest: “creATed↗, conTROLLED↗, MANaged↗, and MADE to SERVE a PURpose↘”.
-ed endings: created /ɪd/, controlled /d/, managed /d/, started /ɪd/, emphasizes (third-person /ɪz/).
Organisers as their own tone units: “FIRSTly, | …”, “SECondly, | …”; “HOWever, | alLAH SEES and KNOWS EVerything”.
Word focus: EV-i-dent-ly, ev-er-LAST-ing, un-WOR-thy, RA-tion-al, dis-ap-PEAR-ance, EM-pha-sizes.
beforeReading: Show the two words “sign” and “god” and ask: “Can something be a sign of a thing without being that thing?” Collect everyday examples (smoke is a sign of fire).
duringReading: Collect the words that describe the heavenly bodies.
Mark what comes before and after “However”.
Two boxes: firstly / secondly.
Underline the sentence where the conflict starts.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge using the two boxes.
Language Focus: Match the descriptions (Activity 1), identify the contrast of “However” (Activity 2), reorganise the two-part explanation and the sequence (Activity 3).
Write the Activity 4 contrast-and-reframing paragraph on a non-story topic.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: “Can something be a sign of a thing without being that thing?” everyday examples; 5–12 Listen and read, collect the descriptive words; 12–18 Card sort in pairs: Eight cards (created, everlasting, come and go, sees and knows everything, managed, without end, fading, made to serve a purpose) into “the heavenly bodies” / “Allah”, then the two-box organiser for Abraham’s clarification; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 in pairs, Activity 2 as whole-class discovery (What is on each side of However?), Activity 3 individually; 31–38 Use: Learners write a contrast-and-reframing paragraph about something often misread, for example a traffic light or a warning symbol that is a sign and not the danger itself, with firstly / secondly and one however; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which words in the first sentence show that the heavenly bodies are created?
What two points does Abraham make, and why is the second one important?
What happens after his rational thinking uncovers the truth?
interactiveTips: Use the “Signs, Not Gods” hotspot for Abraham’s explanation and “The Conflict Begins” hotspot for the start of the conflict.
Replay the verse once and ask learners to list the signs it names.
Keep the conflict at the level the chapter describes (arguing and threatening); do not add events.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Provide the eight cards with pictures or Turkish glosses and the frames “Firstly, ____. Secondly, ____.” and “____; however, ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write the clarification three ways (firstly / secondly; not only … but also; both … and) and say which gives the second point the most weight.

formativeAssessment: Identifies the created / Creator contrast.
States both parts of the clarification.
Reorganises a two-part argument and a sequence with accurate linkers.
expectedResponses: The heavenly bodies are created, controlled and temporary, while Allah knows everything and is everlasting; Abraham explained that they are unworthy of worship and that they are signs of Allah, and after his reasoning uncovered the truth, the conflict with the star worshippers began.
content.transferTask: Choose a symbol at school (a bell, a flag, a sign) and write two sentences: Firstly what it is not, secondly what it is a sign of.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover the created / Creator contrast from the participles, and did they keep both parts of Abraham’s clarification?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, sort the eight cards into “the heavenly bodies” and “Allah”. Then complete the two-box organiser for Abraham’s clarification.
checkQuestions: How many cards? (eight)
How many boxes in the organiser? (two)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that “made to serve a purpose” goes with the heavenly bodies. In Activity 2, ask what is on each side of However. In the Use task, check firstly and secondly.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “not only that … but also that …” and one beginning “After …, …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Identifies the created and Creator contrast.
rubricLevels.notYet: Read two cards and ask which side each belongs to.

rubricLevels.secure: States both parts of the clarification.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Are they worthy of worship? What are they signs of?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Organises the argument with firstly, secondly and however.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the three markers in order.

rubricLevels.secure: Controls the sequence with after.

interculturalFocus.notice: Abraham says the heavenly bodies are signs, not gods. Symbols carry different meanings in different cultures.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: The crescent and star appear on the Turkish flag. What does the moon mean in Turkish culture, and what does it mean in English expressions ('once in a blue moon', 'over the moon')?
interculturalFocus.perspective: A symbol has meaning only inside its culture. Learners explain one Turkish symbol to a foreign visitor without assuming they already know it.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note the two points Abraham made.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners explain Abraham’s two points in two sentences.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner tells a partner how the star worshippers answered. The partner says why.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentence with “firstly” and “secondly”. Listener notes the two points. Writer writes them.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visitor asks, “How do you explain a big idea with simple logic?” The learner answers and links it to Abraham.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Abraham (pbuh)'s rational thinking helped to uncover the truth, and then the conflict between him and the worshippers of the stars and planets started.” into their home language. How did each pair render “uncover”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what Abraham said about the stars and planets. Next lesson ask what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The writer uses ‘firstly’ and ‘secondly’. Why are these words useful here?” (They make the argument clear.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give both points. They talk about the verse in their own words.

objectives: Follow Abraham’s argument in Surah al-An’am 80–83: his guidance, his lack of fear, his questions and the final question about security.
Separate what the verses say from the writer’s comments and inferences after the quotation.
Discover rhetorical questions, the narrow exception with “unless”, and ways of framing an inference (That … shows …, The fact that …, It is understood from … that …).
Build a question-led argument that distinguishes evidence from inference.
content.pedagogy: The chapter is one long quotation followed by three sentences of commentary. Learners first mark where the quotation ends. Then they sort sentences into “from the verses” and “the writer’s comment or inference” and discover the signals themselves: “attempted to”, “That … shows …”, “It is understood from … that …”. For the exception you ask: “Is Abraham afraid of the partners? Then what does ‘unless my Lord wills it’ add?” The verses are read and explained, never gapped or rewritten.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 10 conflict; if / unless; questions that expect no answer, in Turkish and in English.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Unless my Lord wills it” does not mean Abraham is sometimes afraid; it limits what can happen to him to his Lord’s will.
The threat of punishment “of their gods” is the writer’s inference from Abraham’s words, not a line quoted from the people.
The people’s arguments are not quoted; the writer comments on their absence.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: rhetorical questions (Will you not reconsider? So which of the two parties has more right to security, if you are aware?) · exception with unless = except if · evidence vs inference (attempted to …; That these arguments are not told … shows …; It is understood from … that …) · The fact that … as a clearer subject · We understand / infer from … that ….
Notice (Activity 1): pairs sort six parts into “from the verses” and “the writer’s comment or inference”. Ask: “Which words show you the writer is now speaking?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Decide what “unless my Lord wills it” does to the main claim; then rewrite the that-clause subject with “The fact that …” and the impersonal passive with “We understand / infer …”.
Likely errors: *unless my Lord does not will it (double negative) · *That these arguments are not told shows … read as a quotation · *It understands from … that … · treating an inference as a stated fact.
Use (Activity 4): an 8–10 sentence argument about a non-story disagreement with two rhetorical questions, one unless-exception, one sentence about evidence or authority, one marked inference and a final comparison of which position is better supported.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Rhetorical questions fall rather than rise because the speaker expects no answer: “WILL you NOT reCONsider↘?”, “So WHICH of the TWO PARties | has MORE RIGHT to seCURity↘, | if you are aWARE?”
The exception as a separate tone unit: “I do NOT FEAR partners you asSIGN to him, | unLESS my LORD WILLS it.”
Weak forms in the framing sentence: “It is UNderSTOOD from …” /ɪt ɪz/.
Word focus: com-pre-HENDS, au-THOR-i-ty, se-CUR-i-ty, ri-DIC-u-lous-ness, cor-RECT-ness, THREAT-ened.
beforeReading: Write two sentences on the board: “He is late. He must have missed the bus.” Ask: “Which one is a fact and which one is a conclusion someone draws?” Learners suggest words that signal an inference (must, probably, so we can say …).
duringReading: Mark where the quotation from Surah al-An’am ends.
Underline the questions in the verses.
Circle “unless”.
Highlight the writer’s three comment sentences and the signal word at the start of each.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge and name whether your evidence comes from the verses or from the writer.
Language Focus: Sort quotation and commentary (Activity 1), explain the unless-exception (Activity 2), reframe the inferences (Activity 3).
Write the Activity 4 question-led argument on a non-story disagreement.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Fact or conclusion? two board sentences, learners name the signal of inference; 5–12 Listen to the verses, then read and mark where the quotation ends; 12–18 Evidence table in pairs: left column a line from the verses, right column the writer’s comment on it, with the signal word circled; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 in pairs, Activity 2 as whole-class discovery (Is Abraham afraid? What does unless add?), Activity 3 individually; 31–38 Use: Groups of three prepare a short question-led argument on a school debate (for example homework at weekends) with two rhetorical questions, one unless and one “It can be inferred that …”, and one group reads to the class; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What questions does Abraham ask, and what answer does he expect?
Which information comes from the verses and which from the writer’s interpretation?
How does the writer use the absence of the people’s arguments?
interactiveTips: Use the “Who Deserves Security?” hotspot for the question about security and the “Empty Arguments” hotspot for the writer’s commentary on the people’s arguments.
Replay the verses without stopping, then replay only the last three sentences of the chapter.
Do not invent the people’s arguments; the chapter says they are not told.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a two-column table with the verse lines already copied and the frames “The verses say that ____.” and “The writer infers that ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Rewrite the three commentary sentences with three different inference frames (It can be inferred that …, This suggests that …, We conclude from … that …) and rank them by strength.

formativeAssessment: Separates quotation from commentary accurately.
Explains unless as a narrow exception that keeps the claim.
Marks an inference explicitly in their own writing.
expectedResponses: In the verses Abraham says he does not fear the partners, unless his Lord wills it, and asks which side has more right to security; the writer then comments that the people’s arguments are not told and infers from Abraham’s words that they threatened him with the punishment of their gods.
content.transferTask: Read a short news headline and write one sentence stating what it says and one sentence that marks your inference from it.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners find the boundary between quotation and commentary themselves, and did they mark their own inferences?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, make an evidence table: a line from the verses on the left, the writer’s comment on the right. Circle the signal word.
checkQuestions: What goes on the left? (a line from the verses)
What do you circle? (the signal word)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check where the quotation ends in each pair’s marking. In Activity 2, listen for unless as a narrow exception. Have one group read their argument and the class name the inference frame.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “unless” and one beginning “It can be inferred from … that …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Separates quotation from commentary.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Are these Abraham’s words or the writer’s?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains unless as a narrow exception.
Marks an inference with “It can be inferred that …”.
Builds a question-led argument.

interculturalFocus.notice: Abraham argues with rhetorical questions. Debate styles differ across cultures.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: How do people debate on Turkish TV, and how do formal debates work in British schools (the Oxford-style debate with rules and time limits)? Which style helps people listen better?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners compare debate styles, not nations. They practise one rule from formal debating: let the other side finish.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note the argument and what the writer says about it.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners explain in two sentences why the people’s arguments are not told.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner explains to a partner what the people threatened Abraham with. The partner says how we know.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Finder finds the sentence about the ridiculousness of their claims. Reader reads it aloud. Explainer paraphrases it.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A classmate asks, “How do you stay calm when someone threatens you in an argument?” The learner answers and links it to Abraham.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “His people attempted to argue with him and present evidence to prove the correctness of their beliefs.” into their home language. How did each pair render “attempted to”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, how Abraham argued for Tawhid. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The writer reads meaning from what the verses do not say. What does this show about the writer’s method?” (Silence in the text can carry meaning.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners explain the writer’s comment. They do not translate the verses.

objectives: Explain how Abraham responds to the threat: He pays no heed, declares that benefit and harm come from Allah and calls people to worship Him alone.
Follow the exchange in Surah al-Anbiya 52–56 and say what each line does in the debate.
Discover fixed expressions with prepositions (pay no heed to, mindful of, faithful to), not only … but … as well with inversion, and reported instructions vs imperatives.
Describe a response to pressure that is based on a clear principle.
content.pedagogy: Give each pair the five lines of the verse on strips and ask them to order them by what each line does (question, justification by tradition, answer, doubt about seriousness, statement of belief). The debate structure becomes visible before any grammar. The expressions are discovered in context: Learners find the preposition that belongs to each one (heed to, mindful of, faithful to) and notice that the verse moves “to” to the front. Inversion after “Not only” is discovered by comparing the text sentence with a version that starts with “Not only”.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 11 threat; not only … but also; told + person + to.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “We found our parents worshipping them” justifies the practice by tradition; it is not evidence that the statues are gods.
“Are you telling us the truth, or are you just playing?” questions Abraham’s seriousness; it does not accept his view.
The father was the most amazed and furious because he also shaped and sold idols, not only because he worshipped them.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: debate functions in the verse (challenging question → tradition → direct answer → doubt → statement of belief and witness) · fixed expressions with prepositions (paid no heed to, mindful of, to which you are faithful, in evident error) · not only … but … as well and inversion (Not only did he worship idols, but …) · reported instruction (told them to firmly reject …) → imperative.
Notice (Activity 1): pairs order the five lines and label what each line does. Ask: “What do the people use as their reason? Does Abraham accept that reason?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Match the expressions and underline their prepositions; then start the father sentence with “Not only …” (what changes after it?) and turn the reported instruction into direct speech.
Likely errors: *paid no heed this threat · *faithful with · *Not only he worshipped idols, but … (no inversion) · *He said to them, “To reject …”.
Use (Activity 4): an 8–10 sentence paragraph on a non-story situation in which someone faces pressure and responds from a principle, with “As a …”, “In doing so”, a short exchange of challenge and response, and not only … but also.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Read the exchange with clear speaker changes and a short pause between turns; the question “WHAT are these STATues | to which you are FAITHful?” falls at the end.
Inversion with stress on the auxiliary: “NOT ONly DID he WORship IDols, | but he SHAPED and SOLD them as WELL.”
Weak forms: “to” /tə/, “of” /əv/ in “mindful of the oneness of Allah”.
Word focus: MIND-ful, EV-i-dent, FAITH-ful, WIT-ness, a-MAZED, FU-ri-ous.
beforeReading: Ask: “If someone says ‘We have always done it this way’, is that a reason? When is it a good reason and when is it not?” Collect one example of each.
duringReading: Underline what Abraham declared about benefit and harm.
Number the five lines of the verse and write the function next to each.
Circle the fixed expressions and their prepositions.
Mark why the father was the most furious.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the numbered lines in view.
Language Focus: Order the debate (Activity 1), match the expressions of response and conflict (Activity 2), then add with inversion and turn the instruction into direct speech (Activity 3).
Write the Activity 4 stance-and-response paragraph about a non-story situation.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: “We have always done it this way” — a good reason or not? one example of each; 5–12 Listen and read; 12–19 Strip task in pairs: Order the five verse lines and label each one (question / tradition / answer / doubt / belief), then compare with another pair; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–32 Language Focus: Activity 1 as a quick check of the strip task, Activity 2 in pairs with a preposition race (heed to, mindful of, faithful to), Activity 3 as whole-class discovery (What happens to the word order after Not only?); 32–38 Use: Learners write the Activity 4 paragraph about a student who keeps to a fair-play principle under team pressure, with “As a …”, “In doing so”, a two-line exchange and not only … but also; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How does the chapter describe Abraham’s response to the threat?
What reason do the people give for their worship, and how does Abraham answer it?
Why was his father the most amazed and furious?
interactiveTips: Use the “No Fear of Idols” hotspot for Abraham’s response and “The Angry Idol Maker” hotspot for his father’s reaction.
Replay the verse and ask learners to raise a hand at each change of speaker.
Treat the verse lines as quotations: explain and order them, never gap or rewrite them.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the five strips with the function labels in a box to match, and the frames “He paid no heed to ____.” and “Not only did ____, but ____ as well.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short dialogue on a non-story topic that follows the same five functions (question, tradition, answer, doubt, statement) and label each line.

formativeAssessment: Orders the debate and names each function.
Uses fixed expressions with the correct preposition.
Produces inversion after “Not only”.
expectedResponses: Abraham ignored the threat, declared that benefit and harm come from Allah and told the people to reject idol worship; when they justified it by their parents’ practice, he said they were in evident error and bore witness that their Lord created the heavens and the earth; his father was the most furious because he also shaped and sold idols.
content.transferTask: Write two sentences about a time someone paid no heed to pressure: One with “As a …” and one with “In doing so, …”.
content.teacherReflection: Did the strip task make the debate structure visible, and did learners discover the inversion from the example rather than from a rule?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, put the five verse lines in order and label each one: question, tradition, answer, doubt or belief. Then compare with another pair.
checkQuestions: How many labels? (five)
Who do you compare with? (another pair)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that the parents’ practice is labelled tradition. During the preposition race, note the most common errors. In Activity 3, listen for inversion after Not only.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “paid no heed to” and one beginning “Not only did …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Orders the debate and names each function.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the five labels on cards.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses fixed expressions with the correct preposition.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the three expressions with the preposition missing.

rubricLevels.secure: Produces inversion after Not only.
rubricLevels.notYet: Model “Not only did he …, but he also …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes a response based on a principle.

interculturalFocus.notice: Abraham pays no heed to threats and says benefit and harm come from Allah. Courage to stand by one's beliefs under pressure is valued in many cultures.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which expressions describe this courage in English ('stand your ground', 'stick to your principles') and in Turkish ('Doğru söyleyeni dokuz köyden kovarlar')? What does each proverb suggest about society?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners notice that proverbs sometimes show the cost of honesty. They discuss the proverb, not their own family conflicts.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note Abraham’s fear of Allah and his words to his people.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners explain in two sentences why his father was the most furious.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner tells a partner what Abraham declared about benefit and harm. The partner says it in simpler words.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the last paragraph. Listener notes the three things his father did. Writer writes them.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visitor asks, “What happens when a person’s belief goes against his family’s work?” The learner answers carefully.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “A bitter struggle began between Abraham (pbuh) and his people.” into their home language. Which word did each pair choose for “bitter”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, why the struggle between Abraham and his people began. Next lesson ask what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why does the writer end with his father ‘shaped and sold them as well’?” (His work and money were also at risk.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give the three things his father did. They explain the verse in their own words.

objectives: Explain how Abraham advises his father with respect: Sense of duty, avoiding embarrassment, expressing love, then asking kindly.
Follow the verse from Surah Maryam: the question, the invitation, the warning and the concern.
Discover “I fear that …” for a worried prediction, compact purpose and reason (to save, Being a wise son, hoping to …), and careful reporting (or after could not, why he worshipped, before he got).
Write a respectful persuasion that manages both the argument and the relationship.
content.pedagogy: Frame the chapter as a lesson in respectful persuasion. Pairs list Abraham’s moves in order (duty → no embarrassment → love → kind question → quick explanation) and decide what each move protects: The argument or the relationship. The verse is then read in four parts (question, invitation, warning, concern). To discover the stance you ask: “Does Abraham say the punishment will certainly come? Which words tell you?” Learners find “I fear that …” before you name it. Remind the class that the verse continues into Chapter 14.
priorKnowledge: so that; so for result; reported questions from Chapter 6.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “I fear that a punishment … will afflict you” expresses concern, not certainty.
Abraham does not make fun of his father’s job; the chapter says he avoided embarrassing him.
The father’s last question is not an agreement; the exchange continues in the next chapter.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: stance with I fear that … will … · purpose (so that his father could be saved → to save / in order to save) · reason (He was a wise son, so … → Being a wise son / As he was …) · hoped-for effect (in that way, he hoped to … → hoping to …) · careful reporting (could not hear, see, or protect · asked him why he worshipped · Before his father got angry).
Notice (Activity 1): Read the warning line and ask: “Is the punishment presented as certain? What does ‘I fear that’ tell us about Abraham’s feeling?” Learners judge the statement false and explain it before you confirm.
Build (Activities 2–3): Rewrite purpose, reason and hope in compact forms, then choose or / worshipped / got and explain why nor, did he worship and will get fail here.
Likely errors: *could not hear, see, nor protect · *asked him why did he worship · *Before his father will get angry · *Being a wise son, so he did not ….
Use (Activity 4): an 8–10 sentence paragraph about a non-story situation in which someone tries to persuade a person they respect, with so that, “in that way”, neither … nor …, one invitation and one carefully framed possible consequence (I’m concerned that … / I fear that …).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Address forms as their own tone unit with a warm, falling tone: “O my FAther, | …”.
Parallel negatives with equal stress: “NEIther HEAR, | nor SEE, | nor BENefit you in ANy way”.
Concern, not threat: “I FEAR that | a PUNishment …” spoken softly, with a slight fall.
Word focus: em-BAR-rassed, FA-ther-ly, dis-o-BE-di-ent, be-NEF-i-cent, af-FLICT, PUN-ish-ment.
beforeReading: Ask pairs: “How would you tell an older family member that you disagree with a habit of theirs, without hurting them?” Collect three strategies on the board to compare with Abraham’s moves.
duringReading: List Abraham’s moves in order.
Divide the verse into question / invitation / warning / concern.
Underline “I fear that”.
Mark the words that show kindness (kindly, loved, wise son).
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the list of moves in view.
Language Focus: Judge “I fear that” (Activity 1), compact purpose, reason and hope (Activity 2), choose the careful reporting forms (Activity 3).
Write the Activity 4 respectful persuasion paragraph on a non-story situation.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: Three strategies for disagreeing with an older family member; 5–12 Listen and read; 12–19 Moves timeline in pairs: Abraham’s five moves with a quote each, then compare with the class strategies (which one did the class not think of?); 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–32 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Certain or a worry?), Activity 2 in pairs, Activity 3 individually with a short explanation of “or” vs “nor”; 32–38 Use: Learners write a respectful persuasion paragraph to a friend who is spending too much time online, with so that, in that way, neither … nor … and “I’m concerned that …”; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does Abraham tell his father that he loves him before asking his question?
What does the verse invite the father to do, and what does it warn about?
How is “I fear that …” different from “I know that …” in this situation?
interactiveTips: Use the “Gentle Advice” hotspot for Abraham’s gentle motive and the “A Warning About Satan” hotspot for his warning about Satan.
Replay the verse and pause after each “O my father” so learners name the function.
Keep the verse as a quotation; persuasion practice happens only in the non-story Use task.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frames “He wanted to advise his father so that ____.”, “He did not ____ or ____.” and “I’m concerned that ____ will ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write two versions of the same message to a friend, one harsh and one respectful, and explain which language choices change the relationship.

formativeAssessment: Lists Abraham’s moves in order with evidence.
Explains “I fear that” as concern rather than certainty.
Uses compact purpose and reason forms accurately.
expectedResponses: Abraham felt it was his duty to advise his father so that he could be saved; he did not embarrass him, told him he loved him and asked kindly why he worshipped statues that could not hear, see or protect him, then invited him to follow him and warned, with concern, of a possible punishment.
content.transferTask: Write a three-sentence message that gives advice to someone older than you: One sentence of respect, one reason, one concern with “I’m worried that …”.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners notice how language choices protect the relationship, and did they read the verse as a quotation rather than material for role-play?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, put Abraham’s five moves on a timeline with a quote for each. Then compare them with our class strategies: which one did we not think of?
checkQuestions: How many moves? (five)
What do you compare them with? (the class strategies from the hook)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that “did not embarrass him” and “told him he loved him” appear as moves. In Activity 1, listen for “I fear that” read as concern. In the Use task, check that the tone stays respectful.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “so that” and one with “I fear that …” or “I’m concerned that …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Lists Abraham’s moves in order with evidence.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the five moves on cards.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains “I fear that” as concern, not certainty.
Uses so that and in that way for purpose and reason.
Writes a respectful persuasion paragraph.

interculturalFocus.notice: Abraham advises his father with love and respect before he asks his question. Speaking to elders follows different politeness rules in different cultures.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: How would you start a difficult message to an older relative in Turkish (Babacığım, sizi çok seviyorum ama …)? How in English (Dad, I love you, and I'm worried that …)? Which softeners does each language use?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners avoid saying English is 'cold' or Turkish is 'emotional'. Each language has its own polite tools; learners practise both.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note how Abraham spoke to his father.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners explain in three sentences how Abraham showed respect to his father.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner explains to a partner why Abraham told his father that he loved him. The partner says what he hoped for.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the first four sentences. Listener notes the polite steps. Writer writes them in order.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A classmate asks, “How do you give advice to an older person in your culture?” The learner gives two polite ways and links them to Abraham.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “He was a wise son, so he did not make his father feel embarrassed, or make fun of his job.” into their home language. How did each pair render “make fun of”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, how Abraham gave advice to his father. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener said about advice.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The writer explains Abraham’s manner before giving the verses. Why?” (The reader sees how he spoke before reading what he said.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners name the polite steps. They talk about the verses in their own words.

objectives: Contrast the father’s threat and demand with Abraham’s calm promises and hope.
Explain why Abraham went to the town to debate although he knew he might face negative consequences.
Discover how “will” carries both a threat and a commitment, how “might” marks possible risk and how “Just as A …, or B …, C …” builds an analogy.
Write a risk-aware reasoning paragraph that uses an analogy to explain a method.
content.pedagogy: The chapter begins in the middle of the verse from Chapter 13, so first recall the father’s question. Then learners sort the lines into “threat or demand” and “promise or hope” and discover that the same future form serves opposite purposes. The ending is a comparison: pairs draw three boxes (doctor / judge / Abraham), write what each one looks for and why, and see that the analogy presents questioning as a careful method. The verse is read and explained, never gapped.
priorKnowledge: First conditional; will for promises; might for possibility.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Abraham’s “will” sentences are promises about his own actions, not threats.
“He knew well that he might face negative consequences” means the risk was possible, not certain.
The doctor and the judge are comparisons for his method; they are not characters in the story.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: will for a threat (If you do not stop this, I will stone you) vs will for a commitment (I will ask my Lord to forgive you) · imperative as a demand (So leave me alone …) · I hope I will … for hopeful stance · might for a possible risk (he knew well that he might face …) · analogy with Just as …, or …, … and purpose infinitives (to find, to uncover, to reveal).
Notice (Activity 1): pairs sort the lines into threat/demand and promise/hope. Ask: “Both speakers use ‘will’. Why do the two sets of sentences feel so different?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Decide what “might” shows about Abraham’s decision, then match each part of the doctor and judge comparison with its meaning.
Likely errors: *he knew well that he must face (certainty instead of possibility) · *Just like a wise doctor looks … (like + clause in formal writing) · *to reveal of the reality · reading Abraham’s “will” as a threat.
Use (Activity 4): an 8–10 sentence paragraph on a non-story situation where someone continues despite possible consequences, with one condition → consequence, two will-commitments, one might and one “just as” analogy ending with a purpose (to uncover …).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Contrast the tones: The threat with strong stress and a falling tone, “I WILL STONE you↘”; the promise softer, “I will ASK my LORD | to forGIVE you”.
Possibility: “he KNEW WELL | that he MIGHT FACE | NEGative CONsequences” (stress on MIGHT).
Analogy in three tone units: “JUST as a WISE DOCtor … | or a CLEVer JUDGE … | ABraham QUEStioned them …”.
Word focus: dis-ap-POINT-ed, de-TER-mined, CON-se-quen-ces, SUS-pect (noun), un-COV-er, re-VEAL.
beforeReading: Recall the end of Chapter 13: Abraham (pbuh) fears that his father will become a friend of Satan. The father now answers (“Are you rejecting my gods, O Abraham?”). Ask: “How do you think each of them will answer now?” Pairs predict one sentence for the father and one for Abraham.
duringReading: Two colors: The father’s threat and demand / Abraham’s promises and hope.
Underline “In fact, he knew well that he might …”.
Box the doctor and the judge and what each one looks for.
Mark why Abraham went to the town.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge using the two colors.
Language Focus: Sort threat and promise (Activity 1), interpret “might” (Activity 2), match the parts of the analogy (Activity 3).
Write the Activity 4 risk-aware reasoning paragraph on a non-story situation.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Recall the father’s last question and predict both answers; 5–11 Listen and read; 11–18 Two-color sort in pairs, then a whole-class discussion: Same “will”, different purpose; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Why do the two “will” sets feel different?), Activity 2 in pairs, Activity 3 with a three-box board (doctor / judge / Abraham: looks for / in order to); 31–38 Use: Learners write a risk-aware paragraph about a student reporter investigating a problem in the canteen, with might, two will-commitments and a “just as” analogy; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How does Abraham answer his father’s threat?
What does the chapter say Abraham knew before he went to the town?
What do the doctor and the judge have in common with Abraham’s questioning?
interactiveTips: Use the “A Father’s Threat” hotspot for the father’s threat and the “Questions Like a Judge” hotspot for Abraham’s questions.
Replay Abraham’s answer and ask learners to count his “will” sentences.
Do not role-play the threat; read the verse as a quotation.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a sorting table with the lines already copied and the frames “He knew that he might ____.” and “Just as a ____ ____ to ____, ____ ____ to ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Create a new analogy for careful questioning (for example a scientist or a mechanic) in the “Just as …” pattern and explain why it fits.

formativeAssessment: Distinguishes threat from commitment with evidence.
Explains might as possibility.
Builds a coherent analogy with a purpose.
expectedResponses: The father threatened to stone Abraham, but Abraham answered with peace, a promise to ask forgiveness for him and a hope in his prayer; although he knew he might face negative consequences, he went to the town and questioned the people, like a doctor looking for a cause or a judge seeking the truth.
content.transferTask: Write one analogy that explains why asking questions is useful in your favorite school subject, using “Just as …”.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover that the same form can threaten or promise, and did the analogy help them explain the method rather than the conflict?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, sort the will-sentences in two colors: the father’s threat and Abraham’s commitments. Then discuss with the class why the same will feels different.
checkQuestions: How many colors? (two)
What do we discuss? (why the same will has different purposes)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that “I will stone you” and “I will ask forgiveness” are in different colors. During the three-box board, listen for in order to. In the Use task, check for might.

exitTicket: Write one promise with “will” and one risk with “might” about a plan of yours.

rubricLevels.secure: Tells a threat from a commitment with evidence.
Explains might as possibility.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Was he sure about the consequences?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Builds the doctor and judge analogy with a purpose.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “just as a doctor looks for …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes coherent reasoning about risk.

interculturalFocus.notice: Abraham compares questioning to a doctor or a judge. Professional roles that ask questions exist in every society.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: How do doctors talk to patients in Türkiye and in the UK (the doctor decides, or the doctor and patient decide together)? What does this tell us about cultural expectations?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners describe expectations they have observed and mark their guesses as guesses.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note the father’s answer and Abraham’s method.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners explain the comparison with a doctor and a judge in two sentences.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner explains to a partner why the father’s harsh words did not stop Abraham. The partner gives the reason.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Finder finds the long comparison. Reader reads it aloud. Explainer says what Abraham did with his questions.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visitor asks, “How do good doctors or judges find the truth?” The learner answers and links it to Abraham.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Abraham (pbuh) kindly spoke to his father with clear logic and sense.” into their home language. Which words did each pair choose for “logic and sense”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, how Abraham answered his father’s threat. Next lesson ask what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why does the writer use two comparisons, a doctor and a judge?” (Both look for the truth with careful questions.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners explain both comparisons. They do not translate the verses.

objectives: Explain how Abraham tests the idols with questions and a challenge, and how the people defend their belief with tradition.
Describe Abraham’s reply: No fear, a true religion and guidance from the Lord who alone is worthy of worship.

Discover the difference between testing and defending questions, manner and purpose phrases (Showing no fear, to persuade) and the past perfect, “explain that” and “give up + -ing” in reported argument.
Build a balanced evidence-vs-tradition argument that ends without insult.
content.pedagogy: Put a T-chart on the board: Abraham tests / The people defend. Learners place each question with a reason: Can the answer be checked by looking? Grammar grows from this: You ask “Why did the forefathers’ worship happen before the argument, and how does the text show it?” and learners discover the past perfect in reported argument. Point out early that “speechless idols” here means idols that cannot speak.
priorKnowledge: Past perfect; to + infinitive of purpose; give up.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The people admit the idols are lifeless; their reason is tradition, not evidence.
“Dumb” here means unable to speak.
No idol is broken in this chapter; it ends with “Abraham (pbuh) did not give up arguing with the idolaters”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: testing questions vs defending questions (Do the idols see you …? / Are you criticizing our gods …?) · observable test with see if … · manner (showed no fear as he replied → Showing no fear, … / Fearlessly) · purpose (To persuade them …, he challenged → He challenged them to persuade …) · reported argument (had worshipped · explained that … · did not give up arguing) · who-clauses defining the Lord.
Notice (Activity 1): pairs sort six lines into “Abraham tests the idols” and “The people defend their belief”. Ask: “Which questions could someone check just by looking? Which questions change the topic?”
Build (Activities 2–3): rewrite manner and purpose in compact forms, then correct have worshipped → had worshipped, explained them → explained, to argue → arguing.
Likely errors: *explained them that · *did not give up to argue · *their forefathers have worshipped them (tense in report) · *For persuade them.
Use (Activity 4): an 8–10 sentence argument on a non-story habit defended because “it has always been done this way”, with two testing questions, although / even though, a but-contrast, a relative clause for a better alternative and one “see whether …” test, ending in a balanced conclusion.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Testing questions with a clear fall: “DO the IDols SEE you | when you BOW DOWN before them↘?”
Short tone units: “our LORD, | WHO aLONE is WORthy of WORship. | HE is the creATor of the HEAVens and the EARTH, | and HE REGulates ALL afFAIRS of LIFE”.
Contrastive stress: “I am SErious”; “I have ALready CRITicized them”.
Word focus: CRIT-i-cize, FORE-fa-thers, REG-u-lates, per-SUADE, af-FAIRS, WOR-thy.
beforeReading: Ask: “How can you test whether a claim is true without arguing about it?” Collect ideas (look, measure, try it). Keep “test by looking” on the board.
duringReading: T-chart: tests / defends, with every question placed.
Underline the people’s reason and the fact they admit.
Circle the words that show Abraham’s manner.
Box the challenge “see if …”.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the T-chart in view.
Language Focus: Sort testing and defending (Activity 1), rewrite manner and purpose (Activity 2), correct the reported argument (Activity 3).
Write the Activity 4 evidence-vs-tradition argument with a balanced conclusion.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: “How can you test a claim without arguing?” ideas on the board; 5–12 Listen and read; 12–18 T-chart in pairs, then whole-class check: Which side’s questions can be checked by looking?; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as a quick confirmation of the T-chart, Activity 2 in pairs, Activity 3 as whole-class discovery (Which happened first, the forefathers’ worship or the argument?); 31–38 Use: Groups plan an evidence-vs-tradition paragraph about a school habit (for example always sitting in the same seats) with two testing questions and a “see whether …” test, ending with a fair conclusion; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What do the people admit about the idols, and what reason do they still give?
How do Abraham’s questions differ from the people’s questions?
What does Abraham’s challenge ask the people to observe?
interactiveTips: Use “The Forefathers’ Excuse” hotspot for the people’s excuse and the “A Bold Challenge” hotspot for Abraham’s challenge.
Replay Abraham’s long reply and ask learners to count the who-clauses.
Explain “speechless” as “unable to speak”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the six lines on strips for the T-chart and the frames “They admitted that ____, but ____.” and “He challenged them to see if ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write two short paragraphs about the same habit: One that only defends it by tradition and one that tests it with evidence, then comment on the difference.

formativeAssessment: Classifies testing and defending questions with a reason.
Reports the argument with the past perfect and “explain that”.
Ends their own argument with a balanced conclusion.
expectedResponses: Abraham asked whether the idols could see or benefit them; the people admitted the idols were lifeless but said their forefathers had worshipped them; Abraham replied without fear that he had been sent with guidance from the Lord who alone is worthy of worship and challenged them to see if the idols could harm him.
content.transferTask: Choose one claim you often hear and write one question that tests it by observation and one “see whether …” sentence.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover the difference between testing and defending, and did the class keep the discussion respectful?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, make a T-chart: Abraham’s testing questions and the people’s defence. Then decide with the class: which questions can be checked by looking?
checkQuestions: What are the two columns? (testing questions, defence)
What do we decide together? (which questions can be checked by looking)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that “our forefathers worshipped them” is in the defence column. In Activity 3, ask which happened first. In the group plans, look for a fair conclusion.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “did not give up + -ing” and one with “explained that …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Classifies testing and defending questions with a reason.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Can you check this with your eyes?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses manner and purpose phrases such as without fear.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the phrase in the text.

rubricLevels.secure: Reports the argument with the past perfect.
rubricLevels.notYet: Model “They explained that their forefathers had …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Ends with a balanced conclusion.

interculturalFocus.notice: The people defend their worship by tradition. Every culture has a debate between tradition and change.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which tradition in Türkiye has changed in your parents' lifetime (wedding customs, Bayram visits by phone)? Which has stayed? Is the same debate happening in English-speaking countries (for example about royal traditions in the UK)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners show that respecting tradition and testing it with evidence can go together, as the chapter does.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note the questions, the people’s defense and Abraham’s reply.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners explain in two sentences why the people’s defense was weak.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner tells a partner how Abraham answered “Or are you just joking?”. The partner restates it.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Questioner asks “What did Abraham challenge them to see?”. Finder reads the answer. Summarizer paraphrases it.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A classmate asks, “How do you say ‘I am serious’ politely?” The learner gives two ways.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Abraham (pbuh) did not give up arguing with the idolaters.” into their home language. How did each pair render “did not give up”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, how Abraham debated with the idolaters. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The people admit that the idols are lifeless. Why is this important in the debate?” (Their only reason is tradition.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners explain the weakness of the defense. The notes give Abraham’s challenge.

objectives: Follow the exchange in Surah ash-Shu’ara 69–82: Abraham’s questions, the people’s appeal to their ancestors and his description of the Lord of the Worlds.
Explain how the chain of “He who …” lines contrasts the Lord with idols that do not hear, benefit or harm.

Discover parallel “He who …” clauses, the exception “but not so”, the local stance “I hope” and the change of focus between passive and active (Idol worship is hated by Allah / Allah hates idol worship; provide someone with / provide something to).
Write a cohesive evaluation paragraph that uses a relative-clause chain and an exception.
content.pedagogy: Most of the chapter is a quoted verse, so meaning comes first through structure: Learners number the “He who …” lines and give each one a one-word label (Creator, Guide, Provider, Healer, Giver of life and death, Forgiver). Then they compare the chain with the people’s answers. The exception is discovered with one question: “Are all the things they worship enemies to Abraham? Who is the exception?” The final prose sentence shows the narrator retelling the verses; learners compare it with the verse lines. Verses are read, explained and matched, never gapped or rewritten.
priorKnowledge: Relative clauses with who; passive vs active; the people’s appeal to tradition from Chapters 12 and 15.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “But not so the Lord of the Worlds” excludes the Lord from “enemies”; it does not weaken Him.
“I hope” in the last line shows Abraham’s humility about forgiveness; it is not doubt about the Lord.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: parallel “He who …” clauses for a chain of attributes · exception with but not so (so = “an enemy to me”) · local stance with I hope · passive vs active for topic (Idol worship is hated by Allah / Allah hates idol worship) · provide + person + with + thing / provide + thing + to/for + person.
Notice (Activity 1): learners match the five “He who …” lines with what they say about the Lord. Ask: “Why does the verse repeat ‘He who’? What does the repetition contrast with?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Rewrite the last sentence with Allah as subject and with the other pattern of provide; then decide what “but not so” means and what “so” replaces.
Likely errors: *provides human beings food and drink (missing with) · *provides food and drink with human beings · *Allah is hated idol worship · reading “but not so” as “not as great”.
Use (Activity 4): an 8–10 sentence evaluation of a non-story practice, policy or technology with a question that identifies it, two testing questions, one inherited justification, “Have you considered …?”, a three-part relative-clause chain, one exception and one local stance marker, ending with a reasoned conclusion.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Parallel lines with the same rhythm, stress on the verbs: “HE who creATed me, | and GUIDES me. | HE who FEEDS me, | and WAters me.”
The exception with contrastive stress: “they are ENemies to ME, | but NOT SO | the LORD of the WORLDS”.
Stance inserted as a separate low unit: “HE who, | I HOPE, | will forGIVE my SINS …”.
Word focus: res-ur-REC-tion, AN-ces-tors, re-VIVES, GUI-dance, U-ni-verse, man-KIND.
beforeReading: Ask: “If you describe someone only through what they do for others, what kind of sentences do you need?” Model one: “She is the one who …”. Pairs write two more about a person who helps them.
duringReading: Mark each speaker change in the verse.
Number the “He who …” lines and label each one with one word.
Circle “but not so” and “I hope”.
Compare the last prose sentence with the verse lines and tick what it repeats.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the numbered lines in view.
Language Focus: Match the “He who …” lines (Activity 1), change the focus and the pattern of provide (Activity 2), explain “but not so” (Activity 3).
Write the Activity 4 cohesive evaluation paragraph on a non-story practice.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: “She is the one who …” pairs write two sentences about a helpful person; 5–12 Listen to the verses and read, mark the speaker changes; 12–18 Label chain: Pairs number the “He who …” lines and give each a one-word label, then tick which labels the narrator’s last sentence repeats; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 in pairs with the whole-class question (Why repeat He who?), Activity 2 individually, Activity 3 as whole-class discovery (What does so replace? Who is the exception?); 31–38 Use: Learners write an evaluation of a school app or rule with a “which … which … which …” chain, one exception (except / but not …) and “I expect” or “it seems”; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How do the people answer Abraham’s questions, and what do they rely on?
What picture of the Lord does the chain of “He who …” lines build?
Why does Abraham say “I hope” only in the last line?
interactiveTips: Use the “What Do You Worship?” hotspot for Abraham’s questions to his people and “The Lord of the Worlds” hotspot for his description of Allah.
Replay the “He who …” lines and ask learners to tap the desk on each “He”.
Keep the verse whole on screen; match and explain its lines, never gap them.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the six labels on cards to match with the verse lines, plus the frames “Allah hates ____.” and “He provides ____ with ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short description of a person or institution using a five-part “the one who …” chain and one exception with “but not …”.

formativeAssessment: Labels the attributes in the chain accurately.
Explains the exception and what “so” replaces.
Uses both patterns of provide and chooses active or passive for topic.
expectedResponses: The people said they worship idols because they found their ancestors doing so; Abraham said all these are enemies to him except the Lord of the Worlds, who created and guides him, feeds him and gives him drink, heals him, makes him die and revives him, and whom he hopes will forgive his sins.
content.transferTask: Write a three-part “who …” chain describing a person who supports your school, and add one sentence with “I hope …”.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see how repetition builds contrast with the idols, and did they treat the verse as a text to understand rather than to manipulate?

classroomManagement.instructions: Mark where the speaker changes. In pairs, number the “He who …” lines and give each a one-word label. Tick the labels the narrator’s last sentence repeats.
checkQuestions: What do you give each line? (a one-word label)
What do you tick? (the labels the last sentence repeats)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that pairs find the exception “except the Lord of the Worlds”. In Activity 3, listen for what so replaces. In the Use task, check the which-chain and the exception.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “provides … with …” and one with “All … except …” or “but not …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Labels the attributes in the chain accurately.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the labels on cards to match.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains the exception and what so replaces.
Chooses active or passive to keep the topic.
Writes a cohesive evaluation with a which-chain.

interculturalFocus.notice: The 'He who …' chain describes the Lord of the Worlds. Lists of qualities are a common style in religious and poetic texts of many cultures.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which Turkish poems or ilahis use repeated lines like this (Yunus Emre's poems)? Do you know an English poem or song that repeats a structure in each line?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners notice how repetition works in poetry across languages, without comparing the holiness of texts.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note what Abraham said about his Lord in the verses and the writer’s summary.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners list what Abraham’s Lord does in four short sentences.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner explains to a partner the writer’s summary after the verses. The partner gives two examples.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the last two sentences. Listener notes the things Allah does. Writer writes them.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visitor asks, “What blessings do you thank Allah for every day?” The learner answers with the chapter.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “He explained to them the beauty of Allah’s creation, His power, and His wisdom.” into their home language. Did each pair keep the list of three?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what Abraham said about his Lord. Next lesson ask what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The writer sums up the verses in the last sentence. Why is a summary useful after a long quotation?” (It gives the main point clearly.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners list the actions in their own words and do not translate the verses.

objectives: Explain Abraham’s plan: He distances himself, waits for the festival, goes to the empty temple and questions a statue.
Interpret “Why don’t you eat?” as an ironic test, not a real question.
Discover the future seen from the past (was going to, would), the time sequence in a plan (decided to, waited until, then, had gone) and a rhetorical question as a test.
Write a plan-and-test paragraph with clear time relations.
content.pedagogy: Build a plan timeline on the board: resistance → decision → knowledge of the festival → waiting → temple → question → silence. Learners add a quoted phrase to each step. The viewpoint is discovered by asking: “At the moment he made his plan, had the festival happened yet? How does the narrator show this?” Learners find “was going to” and “would”. The irony is discovered from the result sentence: “What did the statue do? So what did the question prove?” The axe is mentioned calmly as part of the narrative; no acting out.
priorKnowledge: Future seen from the past from Chapter 5; past perfect; until.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Abraham does not expect the statue to eat; the question is ironic.
The priests had gone before Abraham arrived; that is why the temple was empty.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: future seen from the past (He knew that there was going to be a great celebration … All the people would attend it) · plan sequence (decided to do …, waited until the city was empty, then …) · past perfect for an earlier event (The priests had also gone …) · rhetorical question as an ironic test (Why don’t you eat?) · However for continued resistance.
Notice (Activity 1): Ask: “Does Abraham really want an answer from the statue? What happens next?” Learners use “The statue kept silent and rigid” as the evidence before you name irony.
Build (Activities 2–3): rewrite the reported ideas as Abraham’s own thoughts (is going to be, will attend), then correct doing → to do, will be → was, have → had.
Likely errors: *decided doing · *waited until the city will be empty · *The priests have also gone · keeping “would” inside Abraham’s own thought.
Use (Activity 4): an 8–10 sentence plan-and-test paragraph on a non-story situation with however, a decision phrase, a purpose clause, was going to / would, an until-clause, one past perfect and an ironic question, ending with what the test revealed.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Future-in-the-past in weak forms: “there was GOing to be /wəz ˈɡəʊɪŋ tə bi/ a GREAT celeBRAtion”; “all the PEOple would atTEND it” /wəd/.
Sequence markers with pauses: “He WAITed | until the CIty was EMPty, | THEN | CAUtiously MADE his WAY to the TEMple.”
Irony in the voice: A calm, level tone on “The FOOD in front of you is getting COLD. | WHY DON’T you EAT?”
-ed endings: distanced /t/, decided /ɪd/, waited /ɪd/, approached /t/, asked /t/.
Word focus: cel-e-BRA-tion, CAU-tious-ly, OF-fer-ings, RI-gid, FES-ti-val.
beforeReading: Ask pairs: “If you want to prove a point without a long argument, what could you do?” Collect two ideas (show a test, a demonstration). Keep them for the chapter.
duringReading: Plan timeline: Seven steps with a quoted phrase each.
Underline “was going to” and “would”.
Circle “until” and “had also gone”.
Box the question to the statue and the sentence that follows it.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge using the timeline.
Language Focus: Interpret the ironic question (Activity 1), turn the reported ideas into Abraham’s thoughts (Activity 2), correct the timing forms (Activity 3).
Write the Activity 4 plan-and-test paragraph on a non-story situation.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: “How can you prove a point without a long argument?” two ideas; 5–12 Listen and read; 12–19 Timeline in groups of three on A4 (seven steps, each with a quote), then one group presents and others correct the order; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–32 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Does he want an answer? What happens next?), Activity 2 in pairs (What did Abraham think at that moment?), Activity 3 individually; 32–38 Use: Learners write a plan-and-test paragraph about a student who tests an advert’s claim that a bag is waterproof, with was going to, until, had + past participle and an ironic question; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did Abraham wait until the city was empty?
What does the silence of the statue show?
How does the narrator show what Abraham knew about the future?
interactiveTips: Use the “An Empty City” hotspot for the timing of the plan and the “Food for the Idols” hotspot for the question to the statue.
Replay the last three sentences and ask learners what the silence proves.
Describe the axe only as the text does; no dramatisation.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the timeline steps on cards to order and the frames “He knew that there was going to be ____.” and “He waited until ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write the plan as Abraham’s own thoughts in the present (There is going to be …, I will …) and then as the narrator’s past account, and list every form that changes.

formativeAssessment: Orders the plan accurately.
Explains the ironic question with the silence as evidence.
Controls future-in-the-past, until and the past perfect.
expectedResponses: Because the idolaters held on to their idols, Abraham decided to show their error; he knew everyone would attend a festival outside the town, waited until the city was empty, went to the temple, where even the priests had gone, and asked a statue why it did not eat, but it stayed silent.
content.transferTask: Write three sentences about a test you once made of a claim (an app, a product, a rumour): what you were going to check, what you waited for, what the result showed.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover the irony from the evidence sentence, and did the timeline make the time relations clear?

classroomManagement.instructions: In groups of three, draw a seven-step timeline on A4 with a quote for each step. One group presents, and others correct the order.
checkQuestions: How many steps? (seven)
What do other groups do? (correct the order)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Give roles: reader, writer, presenter. Check that the priests had gone before Abraham entered. In Activity 2, listen for what Abraham thought at that moment.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “was going to” and one with “waited until …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Orders the plan accurately.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the first and last steps.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses was going to for future in the past.
Explains the ironic question with the silence as evidence.
Writes a coherent test paragraph.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the four forms as a checklist.

interculturalFocus.notice: Abraham waits for the festival when the city is empty. Festivals that take people out of the city exist in many cultures.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Where do people in Türkiye go on long holidays (to their home village, to the coast)? Where do people in the UK go on bank holidays? What happens to the city?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners describe with facts. They avoid assuming every family travels; some stay home.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note Abraham’s plan and the empty temple.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners describe the empty temple in three sentences.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner explains to a partner why Abraham waited until the city was empty. The partner says who else had gone.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Finder finds the word “cautiously”. Reader reads the sentence. Explainer says why he was careful.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A classmate asks, “What is a festival in your town like?” The learner describes it in two sentences.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “The statue kept silent and rigid.” into their home language. Which word did each pair choose for “rigid”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what Abraham found in the empty temple. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The chapter ends with the silent statue. Why is this ending strong?” (The silence answers the question.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: The description has details from the chapter. Learners use “cautiously” correctly.

objectives: Explain what Abraham did in the temple and why: A practical proof of the people’s error.
Follow the people’s reaction: Shock, the search for who did it and the start of the quoted verses.
Discover “for” + clause as reason, “all except one”, the past perfect and “Having fulfilled …” for a completed action, and hung vs hanged, shocked to see, who had done.
Keep narrative, quoted verse and the narrator’s evaluation apart when summarising.
content.pedagogy: The chapter is the turning point of the temple episode. Learners first separate three kinds of text: Quoted verses (as-Saffat 91–92, al-Anbiya 59–67), the narrator’s account of actions and the narrator’s evaluation (“a practical proof of their foolishness”). Then the one statue left standing is treated as a clue: “Why did he leave one? Where did he put the axe?” The reason meaning of “for” is discovered by testing: learners replace “for” with “because” and with “in order to” and decide which keeps the meaning. The breaking of the idols is summarised calmly and never acted out.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 17 plan; past perfect; except.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “For he knew they would not eat” gives a reason, not a purpose.
He destroyed all the statues except one; the one left matters for the next chapter.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: for + clause = because (He was mocking them, for he knew they would not eat) · exception with all except one · past perfect and perfect participle for a completed task (He had fulfilled his duty … → Having fulfilled …) · hung (objects) vs hanged · adjective + to-infinitive (shocked to see) · who had done that (earlier action in a reported search).
Notice (Activity 1): Ask: “Why was he mocking them? Replace ‘for’ with ‘because’ and then with ‘in order to’: which keeps the meaning?” Learners judge the statement false with their own test.
Build (Activities 2–3): split “all except one” into two statements and put the completed task first with Having fulfilled / After fulfilling; then complete hung / to see / had done and explain why hanged, for seeing and has done fail.
Likely errors: *he hanged the axe · *shocked for seeing · *who has done that · *Having fulfilled his duty, the temple was left (dangling subject).
Use (Activity 4): an 8–10 sentence evidence-building paragraph on a non-story situation with a rhetorical question, a reason with for or because, one exception, a past-perfect completion and a short attributed quotation or piece of evidence, ending with what the evidence shows.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Separate the reason with a pause: “He was MOCKing them, | for he KNEW they would NOT EAT.”
Exception with contrastive stress: “He desTROYED them ALL | exCEPT ONE.”
Past perfect weak form: “He had fulFILLED /həd/ his DUty …”; “who had DONE that”.
Irregular past: hung /hʌŋ/ (not hanged).
Word focus: MOCK-ing, OF-fer-ing, ful-FILLED, PRAC-ti-cal, FOOL-ish-ness, WRONG-do-ers.
beforeReading: Recall the silent statue from Chapter 17. Ask: “If silence proves something, what could make the proof even clearer for everyone?” Collect predictions without confirming them.
duringReading: Three colors: Quoted verse / narrator’s account / narrator’s evaluation.
Underline the reason introduced by “for”.
Mark the exception and where the axe was put.
Circle the people’s first reaction and their question.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the three colors in view.
Language Focus: Test the meaning of “for” (Activity 1), rewrite the exception and the completed task (Activity 2), complete hung / to see / had done (Activity 3).
Write the Activity 4 evidence-building paragraph on a non-story situation.
