Ch31: verse functions (tell, ask a view, accept, promise); Growing up …; must → had to; was to be
Ch32: just as … was about to; promised to; Because of + noun; only; willingness to
Ch33: time frames that limit claims vs Every year; while / whereas; were going to → their plan was to; equivalent to, each other, with longing
Ch34: imperative as a humble request; has commanded / will → had commanded / would; build on; no longer; carry on + -ing
Ch35: was but (= only); not just …; coexisted; evidence limited in place and time; has always been; where for a situation

skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: close reading, evidence selection, quotation vs narrator vs inference, source status, scope, comparison and cross-chapter synthesis.
skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: gist listening followed by targeted replay for evidence, speaker changes in quoted verses, discourse markers, stress and pronunciation.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: evidence-based discussion, respectful challenge, qualification, attribution and sustained B2 explanation using chapter language.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: connected analytical paragraphs on non-story topics with claim–evidence–explanation, source qualification, limited claims and clear time relations.

valuesFocus: D6 Dürüstlük — preserve evidence, source attribution, uncertainty and scope instead of overstating a claim
D10 Mütevazılık — remain open to correction and distinguish conviction from arrogance (Chapters 19–20)
D12 Sabır — sustain purposeful effort when persuasion, search or service is difficult (Chapters 24, 27–29, 31)
D14 Saygı — disagree without humiliating people, as Abraham speaks to his father (Chapters 13–14)
D16 Sorumluluk — connect duty, consultation and shared tasks with responsible action (Chapters 13, 31, 34)
D20 Yardımseverlik — recognize protection, cooperation, provision and service as concrete actions

Use values only where the chapter’s events provide real support, and integrate them into learning activity rather than a detached moral lecture. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.
languageFocus: Every one of the 35 story chapters has an active Language Focus set built as notice → build → use.
Use Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence: Ask what the form does in the text (source, stance, time, cause, scope) before naming it.
Let learners answer first; the explanation shown after each answer confirms the rule they have found.
At B2 the last step is always a connected, non-story paragraph or exchange; the task states which forms to use and learners choose how to organize them.
Quoted verses, hadiths and prayers appear in Language Focus only for reading, matching and explaining; they are never gapped or rewritten.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Keep the same evidence and discourse target while reducing linguistic load for support: sentence strips, sorting tables, frames, audio replay and oral rehearsal. Extend stronger learners through source comparison, rewriting a claim at different strengths, cross-chapter synthesis and explaining their own language choices, not through outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful discussion
notes: Qur’anic verses, prophetic sayings (hadiths), prayers and supplications are read, explained and matched to meanings; they are never gapped, “corrected” or rewritten, and learners do not perform them as drama.
Never depict, draw, role-play or freeze-frame Abraham, Ishmael or any prophet, or the angel Gabriel. Production tasks are always about non-story topics.
Keep the chapter’s distinctions visible: quoted verse, narrator’s account, narrator’s interpretation, reported claims (for example Nimrod’s) and other narrations.

Handle the order against the children (Chapter 5), the breaking of the idols, the fire (Chapters 18–22), the execution of a prisoner (Chapter 23), the dream of sacrifice (Chapters 31–32) and the historical practice of child sacrifice (Chapter 33) calmly and factually; the teacher reads these passages once, and they are never acted out.
Describe the beliefs of Abraham’s people accurately and without mockery; the chapters’ criticism of idol worship is not an invitation to ridicule anyone today.
Do not introduce legends, dates or biographical details that are not in this B2 book.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: The story of Prophet Abraham (pbuh), a fundamental figure in Judaism, Christianity and Islam, raises questions every community faces: How to disagree respectfully, how to check a claim before accepting it, how to live together with people who believe differently, and how shared places and tasks bring people together.

themes.title: Disagreeing with respect:
themes.description: Abraham advises his father kindly, tells him he loves him and does not embarrass him (Chapter 13). Discuss how to disagree with family members, friends or people online without humiliating them.

themes.title: Checking claims with evidence:
themes.description: Abraham tests the idols with questions that can be checked by looking (Chapter 15), and the book separates evidence from tradition. Connect this with checking news, adverts and rumours today.

themes.title: Living together with difference:
themes.description: Chapter 35 says Abraham built a place of worship for all people, not just people of a chosen race or color, and that his faith coexisted with idolatry in the Hijaz. Discuss equal dignity for people of every origin.

themes.title: Shared work and service:
themes.description: Abraham and Ishmael build the Ka’ba together and adapt when the work becomes hard (Chapter 34). Compare this with community projects in which people of different ages share a task.

actions: Write three rules for respectful disagreement in class discussions and online messages, each with an example sentence.
Choose one claim from an advert or a social-media post and write two questions that could test it with evidence.
Plan a small shared class task (for example tidying the school garden or library) in which everyone has a role, and write a short report of how the work was shared.

exitTicket: One claim from today’s chapter, with the sentence that supports it and who says it (the verse, the narrator or a character), is …
One language pattern I noticed today, and what it does to the claim (frames a source, limits, contrasts, shows time), is …
One sentence I can now write about my own world with today’s pattern is …

miniProject.title: Evidence or Tradition?
miniProject.desc: In groups, choose a habit or belief from school or daily life that people defend mainly because “it has always been done this way”. Make a one-page poster or a two-minute audio report: State the claim, write two questions that test it (Chapter 15), report one source correctly (According to …, Some sources say …), mark one inference clearly (It can be inferred that …) and end with a qualified conclusion. Use at least three Language Focus patterns from the book.

reflectivePrompt.title: Speaking Kindly, Standing Firm
reflectivePrompt.desc: Abraham tells his father that he loves him, asks kindly and says “I fear that …” instead of threatening (Chapter 13), and when his father threatens him he answers with peace and a promise to pray for him (Chapter 14). Write eight to ten sentences about a time when you disagreed with someone you respect. How did you express your view? What would you say differently now, and which words would help you stay both honest and kind?

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values genuinely supported by the chapter. Require evidence first, then connect the value to an observable, age-appropriate action. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D6 Honesty
items.value: Source attribution, scope and the difference between evidence and interpretation are made visible in learners’ language.

items.label: D14 Respect
items.value: Abraham’s respectful persuasion of his father models disagreement without humiliation.

items.label: D12 Patience / D16 Responsibility
items.value: Hagar’s search, Ishmael’s answer and the shared building task are linked with patient effort and responsibility.

items.label: D20 Helpfulness
items.value: Provision, protection and shared service are turned into realistic actions at school and at home.

questions: Which part is source evidence and which part is your own application?

cefrProfile.intro: This book is written for CEFR B2. The table links the B2 descriptors of the End-of-Level Test B2 to the chapters of this book where learners practise them.

rows.descriptor: Can read with a large degree of independence, adapting style and speed of reading to different texts and purposes, and using appropriate reference sources selectively.
practice: Chapter 9 (The Signs in the Sky): Fill the rising / setting boxes for the moon and the sun.
Chapter 25 (Emigration and Ishmael’s Birth): Route map: What happened at each stop.
Whole book: Knowledge Check and Final Challenge.

rows.descriptor: Can write clear, detailed texts on a variety of subjects related to his field of interest, synthesising and evaluating information and arguments from a number of sources.
practice: Chapter 3 (Hanifism Before Islam): Write two sentences evaluating a phone, a book or a team “at that time”, so that the reader knows the evaluation belongs to one period only.
Chapter 25 (Emigration and Ishmael’s Birth): Write three sentences about a journey or move you know: One main event, one past-perfect background detail and one “wherever …” pattern.
Language Review, “Use: Argue a School Decision”: Write 6–8 sentences about a decision in your school or town. Plan with a partner first.

rows.descriptor: Can give clear, systematically developed descriptions and presentations, with appropriate highlighting of significant points, and relevant supporting detail.
practice: Chapter 6 (Abraham’s Childhood): Report a short conversation from your week in three sentences: one question, one statement and one request or order.
Chapter 19 (Questioned Before the People): Report a short disagreement from a TV debate or a class discussion in three sentences with “asked if”, “told … to” and “demanded that”.

test.title: End-of-Level Test B2
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the B2 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 85 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.
parts: Reading and Language (50 minutes): in the app. The learner gets a test code at the end.
Writing (35 minutes): on paper. Write an essay discussing this statement: “Travel teaches us more than books do.” (180–220 words)
Speaking (about 10 minutes): one learner with the teacher, in 3 parts.
Scoring: type the test code in “Score a test”, then score Writing and Speaking with the bands. Copy the pilot line for the pilot results sheet.

professionalDevelopment.intro: Use these steps to plan your own development with this book: rate yourself on the EPG areas with this book’s chapters, let a colleague observe one of two lessons, keep a short log after each chapter, run one small classroom enquiry, work with colleagues, and agree on scoring before the End-of-Level Test.

peerObservation.focus: Follow Abraham’s argument in Surah al-An’am 80–83: his guidance, his lack of fear, his questions and the final question about security.
lookFor: Instruction: In pairs, make an evidence table: a line from the verses on the left, the writer’s comment on the right. Circle the signal word.
Check questions: What goes on the left? (a line from the verses) / What do you circle? (the signal word)

While learners work: Check where the quotation ends in each pair’s marking. In Activity 2, listen for unless as a narrow exception. Have one group read their argument and the class name the inference frame.
Evidence of “Quotation vs commentary”: Separates quotation from commentary.

peerObservation.focus: Explain how Abraham ends the debate with the sun challenge and how his fame spreads.
lookFor: Instruction: In pairs, draw scales: Abraham’s effort on one side and the result on the other. Then the class joins both sides in one sentence with however.
Check questions: What goes on the two sides? (effort, result) / What word joins them? (however)
While learners work: Check that “only Sarah and Lot” is on the result side. During the board check, listen for in spite of + noun. In Activity 3, ask what the narrator already knew.
Evidence of “Debate outcome”: States the outcome of the debate.

reflectionLog: After each chapter, answer the chapter’s “After the lesson” question in one or two sentences.
Write down the rubric criterion that most learners had not yet reached and the support you gave.
Every three or four chapters, look at the grammar sequence of this book and plan one short recycling activity for a form learners still avoid.
Before the End-of-Level Test, read your notes and choose two chapters to revise with the class.
standardisation: Before scoring, read the B2 descriptors for written and spoken production in the CEFR table of this book.

With a colleague, score the same three writing papers on your own with the B2 writing bands (Task, Organisation, Grammar, Vocabulary). Then compare and talk about any criterion where your scores differ by more than one band.
Score one speaking test together in the same way: both listen, both score, then compare.
Keep one agreed paper for each band as a sample for later scoring.

selfAssessment.prompt: Chapter 6: Could learners do this by the end of the lesson: “Explain how the chapter presents Abraham’s early wisdom and his first questions about his father’s statues”? Which stage of the lesson flow helped most, and which did not?
Chapter 11 is planned for 40 minutes. Which stage took longer than planned, and what did you move to the next lesson?
Before the pair or group work in Chapter 16, did you ask “What do you give each line?” How many learners could answer before they started?
In Chapter 35, how many learners were secure on “Scope control”? What did you do for those who were not yet secure?

When you asked “Do you know Turkish or Arabic expressions or place names that recall this story (Balıklıgöl in Şanlıurfa)?” in Chapter 21, did learners describe other cultures with facts or with stereotypes? Which words did you give them?

Which of the likely errors listed for Chapter 27 did you hear (*not water · *which they could not see him · *asked him whether had Allah commanded · *here / us not changed to there / them)? Did you correct them during the activity or after it, and why?
Which app tools did your learners use with this book (audio, Word Notes, the exercises and their result codes)? Which one gave you the most useful information about their learning?
Read your reflection log for this book. What is one change you will make the next time you teach this book, and who will you share it with?

actionResearch.question: Do learners use perfect participle clauses (Chapter 18: Having fulfilled …) in their own writing, or only recognise them?
steps: Baseline: in the Chapter 18 transfer task, count learners who write a correct Having + past participle sentence.
Recycle: in Chapters 22 and 34, ask for one sentence that begins with Having … for a completed action.
Check: after the B2 End-of-Level Test, note item 21 (perfect participle clause) for the class in Score a test.
Decide: compare recognition (the test item) with production (the tasks) and plan one rewriting activity.

collaboration: Share your counts for perfect participle clause with another English teacher who uses this book, and agree on one activity to try in both classes.
Plan the Chapter 1 lesson on the three religions that honour Abraham with the religious culture teacher, so both lessons say only what the sources say.

objectives: I can explain why Abraham (pbuh) is a fundamental figure in three religions.
I can tell a statement framed by a source from the writer’s own statement.
I can use a source frame, means and the passive to organize an explanation.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Explain why the opening says “is presented as” (the Qur’an is the source of the portrait, not a sign of doubt), complete three lines with means, also and in detail, and rewrite the title sentences in the passive, starting with the person or with the thing given. The last activity asks you to write a framed explanation of a figure or concept of your own.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: rep-re-SENT-a-tive, mon-o-the-IS-tic, FORE-fa-ther, u-NIQUE. Names: taw-HEED, kha-LEE-lul-lah. Read the long list of prophets at an even pace, with a short pause at each comma.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the Father of Prophets hotspot. Which two sons does it point to? Listen once for the three things that make Abraham (pbuh) central: his belief, his family and his title. Read again and draw the family line from Abraham (pbuh) to Muhammad, Moses and Jesus (pbuh).
discussionPoints: Abraham (pbuh) discovered the oneness of Allah “in the middle of an idol-worshipping nation”. What helps a person keep a clear belief when most people around them think differently?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Messenger of Tawhid” and “Father of Prophets”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the middle of the paragraph and find the sentence about Ishmael (pbuh). Follow the line one step at a time: Isaac, then Jacob, then the later prophets. Match again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write seven to nine sentences about a different historical figure or concept. Frame it with is presented as or is described as, define one idea with means that, add a point with also, and put one title or distinction first with the passive.

whatToNotice: The chapter moves from a definition (monotheistic belief) to a family line (Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob) and ends with a title that no other prophet was given before.

Notice “In the Holy Qur’an, Prophet Abraham (pbuh) is presented as the messenger and representative of the monotheistic belief.” The frame tells you where the portrait comes from; it does not express doubt.
readListen: Before you read, open the Father of Prophets hotspot. Which two sons does it point to?
Listen once for the three things that make Abraham (pbuh) central: his belief, his family and his title.
Read again and draw the family line from Abraham (pbuh) to Muhammad, Moses and Jesus (pbuh).
Open the picture hotspots “Messenger of Tawhid” and “Father of Prophets” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: The chapter has one paragraph. Beginning: Find what monotheistic belief means and the three things Allah has no need of.
Middle: Find the two sons and which later prophets come from each of them.
End: Find the title given only to Abraham (pbuh) and the surah where it appears.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: representative, monotheistic, rival, forefather, unique, Tawhid, idol-worshipping, oneness.
“Prophet Ishmael (pbuh) is the direct forefather of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh).” Why does the word direct matter here?
Write one sentence with representative and one with unique.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will match Ishmael, Isaac and Jacob with what the chapter says about each. The chapter has one paragraph; the answers are in its middle, where the writer moves from Abraham (pbuh) to his sons.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to the middle of the paragraph and find the sentence about Ishmael (pbuh).
Follow the line one step at a time: Isaac, then Jacob, then the later prophets.
Match again.
selfCheck: Can I explain why Abraham (pbuh) matters to three religions?
Can I say what “is presented as” adds to the first sentence?
Can I rewrite “This title was not given to any other prophet before” so that it starts with No other prophet?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write seven to nine sentences about a different historical figure or concept. Frame it with is presented as or is described as, define one idea with means that, add a point with also, and put one title or distinction first with the passive.

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Close the book. Give a one-minute summary from your notes. Then check two names in the story.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “This title was not given to any other prophet before.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, why Abraham (pbuh) is called Allah’s friend.

content.chapter: Chapter 2: Hanifism and the One True Faith
objectives: I can explain what a hanif is and what Hanifism is.
I can tell a definition from an interpretation marked with “We may say that”.
I can explain continuity and change with as, that is and only.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Match four terms with the chapter’s own definitions (Tawhid, a hanif, Hanifism, the acts of worship), decide what “We may say that” adds (a cautious interpretation), and rewrite the reason, the reformulation and the result with because, can find and so. The last activity asks you to explain something with a stable core that changed in its details.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: MIS-sion, REA-son-ing, ca-PAC-i-ties, MOR-al-ly up-RIGHT. Say ha-NEEF with a long second vowel. Read the dash in “the message of Tawhid—the belief …” as a short pause.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the Hanif Path hotspot. Which two qualities make someone a hanif? Listen once: Paragraph 1 is about Abraham’s mission, paragraph 2 about the belief he taught. Read paragraph 2 again and mark the definition, the interpretation, the reason and the conclusion.
discussionPoints: “During his struggle, he had very difficult tests and he passed the tests with his full trust in Allah.” What does trust add when someone faces a very hard test?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “A Life Mission” and “The Hanif Path”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the end of paragraph 2. Find the sentence that begins with As and ends with became necessary. Choose the option that repeats that reason, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write eight to ten sentences about a tradition, system or practice outside the story that kept its core but changed in details. Define one term with a relative clause, add one cautious claim with we may say that, restate one idea with that is, and end with what stayed and what changed.

whatToNotice: The chapter defines its terms in three ways: With a dash (Tawhid), a relative clause (a hanif) and a participle phrase (Hanifism … taught by Prophet Abraham).
Notice “We may say that it is the former version of Islam.” The modal may shows that this is the writer’s careful interpretation, not a definition.
readListen: Before you read, open the Hanif Path hotspot. Which two qualities make someone a hanif?
Listen once: Paragraph 1 is about Abraham’s mission, paragraph 2 about the belief he taught.
Read paragraph 2 again and mark the definition, the interpretation, the reason and the conclusion.
Open the picture hotspots “A Life Mission” and “The Hanif Path” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find his life mission and how he passed his tests.
Paragraph 2: find the two parts of the definition of a hanif and how the existence of Allah can be found.
Paragraph 2: find why details changed and where the only difference lies.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: mission, struggle, morally upright, reasoning, capacities, worship.
“Human beings are capable of discovering Hanifism; that is, the existence of Allah can be found through reasoning.” What does that is do in this sentence?
Write one sentence with struggle and one with capacities.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why some details of the religion changed. The answer is in the last three sentences of paragraph 2; find the reason the writer gives, not the one you might expect.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to the end of paragraph 2.
Find the sentence that begins with As and ends with became necessary.
Choose the option that repeats that reason, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I tell a hanif from Hanifism?
Can I explain why “We may say that” does not introduce a definition?
Can I rewrite the As sentence with because?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write eight to ten sentences about a tradition, system or practice outside the story that kept its core but changed in details. Define one term with a relative clause, add one cautious claim with we may say that, restate one idea with that is, and end with what stayed and what changed.

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Explain Hanifism in three sentences.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “His life mission was to spread the message of Tawhid—the belief that Allah is One and He has no partners.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, what a hanif is.

content.reflectionPrompt: “During his struggle, he had very difficult tests and he passed the tests with his full trust in Allah.” What does trust add when someone faces a very hard test?

objectives: I can explain how Hanifism survived and was later corrupted.
I can explain how “at that time” limits the writer’s evaluation.
I can build a layered sentence with a time clause and participle phrases.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Explain what “at that time” does to the evaluation of Christianity, complete the argument with In fact, However, like and not only, and rebuild the Waraqa–Bilal sentence from its time phrase, main clause and two participle phrases. The last activity asks you to write a contrast-and-extension paragraph about an idea that changed but kept some continuity.
content.pronunciationFocus: Names: WA-ra-qa ibn NAW-fal, bi-LAL al-ha-BA-shi, da-MAS-cus. Stress: cor-RUPT-ed, rev-e-LA-tion, PROPH-et-hood. Say “Ahad, Ahad” slowly and firmly, as a cry.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the Hanifs of the Hijaz hotspot. What did this group stay away from? Listen once and follow Waraqa from Damascus to the desert. Read again and mark In fact, However, like and not only … but also.
discussionPoints: Bilal kept saying “Ahad, Ahad” while he was being punished, and Waraqa answered him. Why can one voice of support matter so much to someone who is suffering for a belief?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “The Hanifs of the Hijaz” and “Bilal’s Cry: “One, One””.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 1 and find Waraqa’s name. Number each event as you read: The journey, the choice of religion, the first revelation, the desert. Order the events again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write eight to ten sentences about a belief, tradition or institution outside the story that changed over time. Use in fact, however, one when or while clause, one relative clause with an evaluation limited by time, and not only … but also to widen your final point.

whatToNotice: The chapter moves from a general claim (three religions based on Abraham’s religion) to a group, then to one person, Waraqa ibn Nawfal, and one scene with Bilal.
Notice “accepted Christianity, which was the least corrupted religion at that time.” The least corrupted is a comparison, and at that time limits it to Waraqa’s period.
readListen: Before you read, open the Hanifs of the Hijaz hotspot. What did this group stay away from?
Listen once and follow Waraqa from Damascus to the desert.
Read again and mark In fact, However, like and not only … but also.
Open the picture hotspots “The Hanifs of the Hijaz” and “Bilal’s Cry: “One, One”” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find who the hanifs of the Hijaz were and what happened to their belief later.
Paragraph 1: find where Waraqa went, what he accepted and how he received the first revelation.
End of paragraph 1 and paragraph 2: find Bilal’s words, Waraqa’s reply and what Islam includes as the last faith.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: idolatry, corrupted, revelation, prophethood, welcomed.
“However, later on, this belief became mixed with idolatry and, like Judaism and Christianity, it was corrupted.” What does like add to the claim?
Write one sentence with corrupted and one with welcomed.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will order four events in Waraqa’s story. All of them are in paragraph 1, from the sentence that names him to the scene in the desert.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 1 and find Waraqa’s name.
Number each event as you read: The journey, the choice of religion, the first revelation, the desert.
Order the events again.
selfCheck: Can I explain what happened to the hanifs’ belief?
Can I explain why the least corrupted is still a comparison?
Can I name the two participle phrases that describe Bilal?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write eight to ten sentences about a belief, tradition or institution outside the story that changed over time. Use in fact, however, one when or while clause, one relative clause with an evaluation limited by time, and not only … but also to widen your final point.

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.

mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, who Waraqa ibn Nawfal was.

content.reflectionPrompt: Bilal kept saying “Ahad, Ahad” while he was being punished, and Waraqa answered him. Why can one voice of support matter so much to someone who is suffering for a belief?

objectives: I can separate what the Qur’an states from what other sources say about Abraham’s birthplace and period.
I can summarise a disputed topic without losing the writer’s caution.
I can use the past perfect, a perfect infinitive and still others correctly.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Sort sentences into those the writer states directly and those reported or hedged, choose the summary that keeps the chapter’s caution, and correct three forms: had existed, to have lived and still others. The last activity asks you to write a qualified overview of a disputed historical topic.
content.pronunciationFocus: Names: A-zer, NIM-rod, SU-mer, mes-o-po-TA-mi-a, har-RAN. Read 20th century BC as the twentieth century BC. Stress: PROS-per-ous, IN-dus-try, his-TOR-i-cal-ly.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the Land of Nimrod hotspot. Which king ruled there? Listen once and count the different sources the writer mentions. Read again and mark every source frame: In the Holy Qur’an, Islamic sources, Some sources say, we can say, is believed.
discussionPoints: Abraham’s message was a belief that “had existed in these lands before, but it had been forgotten over time.” How can an important truth be forgotten by a whole society?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “The Land of Nimrod” and “Many Objects of Worship”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the opening of paragraph 1. Find the words that name the Qur’an and read the next sentence too. Check which options come from “Islamic sources” or “Some sources” instead, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write eight to ten sentences about a partly uncertain historical topic outside the story. Use three source frames (some sources say, is believed to, broadly speaking we can say), one had + past participle, one however, and some … still others … for different groups.

whatToNotice: The chapter sorts its information by certainty: the Qur’an, Islamic sources, some sources, a general conclusion, and what people of that time believed.
Notice “Most generally speaking, we can say that Abraham was born in the city of Ur or Babylon, the country of King Nimrod.” Where sources disagree, the writer offers a careful summary.
readListen: Before you read, open the Land of Nimrod hotspot. Which king ruled there?
Listen once and count the different sources the writer mentions.
Read again and mark every source frame: In the Holy Qur’an, Islamic sources, Some sources say, we can say, is believed.
Open the picture hotspots “The Land of Nimrod” and “Many Objects of Worship” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.

Paragraph 1, middle: Find the two views of the birthplace and the two ways of dating his life.
End of paragraph 1 and paragraph 2: find what had been forgotten and the three kinds of worship in his time.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: birthplace, historically, prosperous, industry, aspects.
“Historically, Abraham (pbuh) is believed to have lived in the 20th century BC.” Why does the writer say is believed instead of simply lived?
Write one sentence with prosperous and one with aspects.

wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to the opening of paragraph 1.
Find the words that name the Qur’an and read the next sentence too.
Check which options come from “Islamic sources” or “Some sources” instead, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I name the fact the Qur’an gives and one claim from other sources?
Can I summarise the birthplace without making it certain?
Can I explain the perfect infinitive after is believed?

content.chapter: Chapter 5: Nimrod’s Fear and Abraham’s Birth
objectives: I can explain why Nimrod feared the birth of Abraham (pbuh).
I can keep two narrations apart without merging them.
I can use was going to and would for the future seen from the past.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.

readListen: Before you read, open the Standing on the Stone hotspot. Why did Abraham need to stand on it?
Listen once for the dialogue and the prayer.
Read paragraph 1 again and mark no longer and carried on.
Open the picture hotspots “Standing on the Stone” and “A Prayer While Building” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find what the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) said about the sacredness of this place.
Paragraph 1: find what Abraham told Ishmael and how Ishmael replied.
End of paragraph 1 and paragraph 2: find what they found, why Abraham stood on Al-Maqam, and what brought him to Mecca.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: made sacred, foundations, handing, response, establish.
“Father and son found the foundations of the old structure and began to build the Ka’ba on it.” What does old structure tell you about the Ka’ba’s history?
Write one sentence with foundations and one with establish.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will order four steps in building the House. All of them are in paragraph 1, from the conversation to the stone of Al-Maqam.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read paragraph 1 from Abraham’s words to Ishmael.
Number each step: the task, the promise, the foundations, Al-Maqam.
Order the steps again.
selfCheck: Can I describe how the work was shared?
Can I explain why Accept is not an order?
Can I report “I will help you for sure” after replied that?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write eight to ten sentences about two people outside the story completing a demanding task. Use has asked or has required, will, a reported instruction, no longer, one continuing parallel action, a cause and adaptation, and a final respectful request.

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Explain in three sentences how they built the Ka’ba.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “Father and son found the foundations of the old structure and began to build the Ka’ba on it.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, how Abraham and Ishmael built the Ka’ba.

content.reflectionPrompt: While they built, father and son prayed, “Accept this service from us”. Why might people who do great work still ask with humility for it to be accepted?

objectives: I can summarise Abraham’s legacy across place, family, worship and guidance.
I can explain how far the chapter’s evidence goes.
I can use has always been and where to connect the past with now.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Match was but the restorer of the structure, the completion of Abraham (pbuh)’s mission, not just people of a chosen race or color and coexisted with idolatry with their meanings, choose the statement that keeps the scope of the evidence sentence, and correct has always been and where. The last activity asks you to write a qualified legacy paragraph.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: re-STOR-er, em-BRACE, com-PLE-tion, co-ex-IST-ed, sal-VA-tion. Read “I will make you a leader to the nations” slowly, as the high point of the chapter.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the Dividing the Lands hotspot. Which son received which land? Listen once for the different kinds of legacy. Read again and mark clear evidence, not just, coexisted and has always been.
discussionPoints: Abraham (pbuh) built a place of worship “for all people, not just people of a chosen race or color.” Where in your own life can you make a place open to everyone?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “A House for Everyone” and “Dividing the Lands”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Find clear evidence near the beginning of paragraph 1. Read the words just before it. Choose the option that names them, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write eight to ten sentences about the legacy of an institution, idea or reform outside the story. Limit one overstrong claim, link evidence to interpretation, use not just, one coexistence statement, when or whenever, and has remained or has continued.

whatToNotice: The chapter limits and widens its claims with care: “He was but the restorer” (only), and “not just people of a chosen race or color” (everyone).
Notice “Reconstruction of the Ka’ba and the call to pilgrimage (see Surah al-Hajj: 27) are clear evidence”. The writer names his evidence and then limits the claim to that region at that time.
readListen: Before you read, open the Dividing the Lands hotspot. Which son received which land?
Listen once for the different kinds of legacy.
Read again and mark clear evidence, not just, coexisted and has always been.
Open the picture hotspots “A House for Everyone” and “Dividing the Lands” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find what the writer calls clear evidence and what it is evidence for.
Paragraph 1: find what Abraham left to each son and what happened to his faith in the Hijaz.
Paragraph 2: find where Abraham died and when he has always been there to show the right path.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: restorer, embrace, completion, coexisted, salvation.
“Reconstructing the Holy Ka’ba was the completion of Abraham (pbuh)’s mission.” How does this sentence link to the rest of the book?
Write one sentence with embrace and one with salvation.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks what the writer presents as clear evidence. Look near the beginning of paragraph 1, at what comes just before those words.
wrongAnswerSupport: Find clear evidence near the beginning of paragraph 1.
Read the words just before it.
Choose the option that names them, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I name three kinds of legacy from the chapter?
Can I explain how far the evidence sentence goes, and where it stops?
Can I explain why has always been links the past and the present?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write eight to ten sentences about the legacy of an institution, idea or reform outside the story. Limit one overstrong claim, link evidence to interpretation, use not just, one coexistence statement, when or whenever, and has remained or has continued.

noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Write a short paragraph on Abraham’s legacy.

mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, why Abraham’s legacy still matters.

metadata.title: Abraham B2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Judge • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 30 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B2 learners who study the story of Prophet Abraham (pbuh) on their own or at home.
learningGoals: Understand the story and the argument of the 35 chapters.
Find evidence in the story before answering.
Tell verses, hadiths and reports from the writer’s interpretation.
Use qualified language when the evidence is qualified.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Listen and read before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text, not with guesses.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 35.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One person in the story I want to remember, and why:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 35 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1: A clear plan helps you keep going and see your progress.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
If you like, choose a weekly goal in your Seyahatname. A new week starts on Monday.
Write one personal goal for this book, for example a skill you want to improve.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week. Short, spaced reviews help you remember.
Before Chapter 1, answer the “I can” statements in section 10, “Look Back”. Answer them again when you finish.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 30 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and hotspots.
Listen and read for the story and the argument.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Listen and Read
sections.text: Use the audio twice: Once for the story and the writer’s point, once to follow the exact wording.
points: First listening: What happens, and what does the writer claim about it?
Second listening: Follow the text line by line.
Replay one long sentence or verse and read it with the same pauses and stress.

sections.title: 4. Evidence or Interpretation?
sections.text: This book mixes verses and hadiths, reports from other sources, and the writer’s own interpretation. Learn to tell them apart.
points: A verse or hadith has a reference, such as (Surah al-Anbiya: 69) or (Sunan an-Nasa’i, 2874).
A report names its source or keeps a distance: Ibn Abbas said …, According to another narration …, Some sources say …, is believed to ….
An interpretation is the writer’s own step: We may say that …, It is understood from … that …, … are clear evidence that ….
Keep your own claims as careful as the evidence: some, almost, at that time, only.

sections.title: 5. Word Notes and Hotspots
sections.text: Each chapter has five Word Notes and two picture hotspots. Use them after you have tried to work out the meaning yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Use the word in a sentence that explains a cause, a contrast or a choice.

sections.title: 6. Quick Challenge and Language Focus
sections.text: Answer the Quick Challenge before reading the feedback. Then do the four Language Focus activities.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): See what a sentence does in the story or the argument.
Activities 2 and 3 (Build or Analyse): choose, correct, rebuild or rewrite forms from the chapter.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say a B2 paragraph about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Work one paragraph or one verse at a time.
Write a one-line summary of each paragraph.
Mark events, sources and interpretations in three colors.
Focus on two Word Notes today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Story
sections.text: The book follows one man who used reason, kept his trust in Allah and stayed kind under pressure. Connect each value to one action.
points: Reason: test a belief by what you can observe (Chapters 8, 9, 15).
Respect: Disagree with a parent without humiliating him (Chapters 13, 14).
Courage: Stand alone for the truth, even before a king (Chapters 19, 23).
Trust and effort: Rely on Allah and still work hard (Chapters 21, 27, 29).
Obedience and consultation: Ask before a hard decision and accept it with patience (Chapters 31, 32).
Equal dignity: A place of worship for all people (Chapter 35).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 35, do the review pages in this order. Go back to the chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Master Glossary
Places & People
Vocabulary Challenge
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back: My Level and My Learning
sections.text: Answer these statements before Chapter 1 and again after the Final Challenge: not yet, partly or yes. They come from the CEFR Companion Volume (Council of Europe, 2020) for level B2. One book is one step towards them, not a test.
points: Reading: “I can read for pleasure with a large degree of independence, adapting style and speed of reading to different texts, using appropriate reference sources selectively.”
Speaking: “I can describe the personal significance of events and experiences in detail.”
Writing: “I can give a review of a film, book or play.”

Mediation: “I can convey detailed information and arguments reliably, e.g. the significant point(s) contained in complex but well-structured texts within my fields of professional, academic and personal interest.”
Which study steps helped me most in this book, and why?
What was hard, and which strategy did I use?
What will I change in my plan for the next book?
